hello.note: Works at any time of day. Casual, to friends: 안녕 (annyeong).

goodbye.note: Said to the person leaving. If you are the one leaving: 안녕히 계세요 (annyeonghi gyeseyo).

please.note: Goes after what you want: 물 주세요 (mul juseyo), water, please. Begging 'please!' is 제발 (jebal).

thank_you.note: Less formal, to friends or people younger than you: 고마워요 (gomawoyo).

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'not at all' – what people really say. Textbook form: 천만에요 (cheonmaneyo).

no.note: Often shortened to 아뇨 (anyo) in speech.

sorry.note: Everyday polite: 죄송해요 (joesonghaeyo). To friends or people younger than you: 미안해요 (mianhaeyo).

excuse_me.note: Also how you call a waiter. To squeeze past: 잠시만요 (jamsimanyo). To interrupt: 실례합니다 (sillyehamnida).

good_morning.note: Many people just say 안녕하세요. To family or a host: 안녕히 주무셨어요? (annyeonghi jumusyeosseoyo?)

how_are_you.note: Literally 'Are you doing well?'. Said as a statement, not a question, it means 'Take care'.

im_fine.note: 덕분에 (deokbune), 'thanks to you', is how Koreans say the 'thank you' here. Plain: 잘 지내요 (jal jinaeyo).

whats_your_name.note: Simpler: 이름이 뭐예요? (ireumi mwoyeyo?). To an elder, replace 이름 with 성함 (seongham).

my_name_is.note: Less formal: 저는 …이에요 (ieyo) after a consonant, …예요 (yeyo) after a vowel.

im_from.note: Also common: 저는 … 사람이에요 (jeoneun … saramieyo), 'I am a … person'.

speak_english.note: Shorter and also common: 영어 하세요? (yeongeo haseyo?)

dont_understand.note: If you just didn't catch the words: 못 알아들었어요 (mot aradeureosseoyo).

speak_slowly.note: To ask them to repeat: 다시 한번 말씀해 주세요 (dasi hanbeon malsseumhae juseyo).

where.note: The bare word is 어디 (eodi). Put the place first: 은행이 어디예요? (eunhaengi eodiyeyo?), where's the bank?

what.note: The bare word is 뭐 (mwo). If you didn't hear someone, say 네? (ne?) with a rising tone.

why.note: The bare word 왜 (wae) on its own sounds blunt.

who.note: The bare word is 누구 (nugu). At the door or on the phone: 누구세요? (nuguseyo?)

where_bathroom.note: In speech the 이 is often dropped: 화장실 어디예요? (hwajangsil eodiyeyo?)

can_you_help.note: 좀 (jom) softens the request, a bit like 'please'.

one.note: Native number, for counting. Prices, dates and phone numbers use 일 (il). Before a noun: 한 (han).

two.note: For prices and dates: 이 (i). Before a noun: 두 (du).

three.note: For prices and dates: 삼 (sam). Before a noun: 세 (se).

four.note: For prices and dates: 사 (sa). Before a noun: 네 (ne).

eight.note: The final ㅂ is silent. For prices and dates: 팔 (pal).

water.note: Asking for it: 물 좀 주세요 (mul jom juseyo). In restaurants water is free, and often self-serve.

coffee.note: Korean has no f sound, so it is 'keo-pi'.

tea.note: Same word as 'car'; context makes it clear. Green tea: 녹차 (nokcha).

bread.note: The doubled pp is tense, with no puff of air.

menu_please.note: Also heard: 메뉴 좀 주세요 (menyu jom juseyo).

bill_please.note: In most Korean restaurants you pay at the counter by the door on your way out.

delicious.note: After a meal, thank the host with 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeotseumnida).

no_meat.note: Soups and broths often contain meat or fish, so it is worth asking.

enjoy_meal.note: Before eating, the diner says 잘 먹겠습니다 (jal meokgetseumnida).

left.note: To a taxi driver: 왼쪽으로 가 주세요 (oenjjogeuro ga juseyo), turn left, please.

right.note: To a taxi driver: 오른쪽으로 가 주세요 (oreunjjogeuro ga juseyo).

straight_ahead.note: To a taxi driver: 직진해 주세요 (jikjinhae juseyo).

want_to_go.note: To a taxi driver: …까지 가 주세요 (…kkaji ga juseyo).

is_it_far.note: From here: 여기서 멀어요? (yeogiseo meoreoyo?). Is it close?: 가까워요? (gakkawoyo?)

one_ticket.note: 장 (jang) is the counter for flat things like tickets.

too_expensive.note: Bargaining at a market: 좀 깎아 주세요 (jom kkakka juseyo).

id_like_this.note: Also: 이걸로 할게요 (igeollo halgeyo), 'I'll take this one'.

pay_card.note: Shorter and very common: 카드 돼요? (kadeu dwaeyo?)

cash.note: Paying in cash: 현금으로 할게요 (hyeongeumeuro halgeyo).

open.note: Many shops simply hang an English OPEN sign.

closed.note: Closed for the day off: 휴무 (humu). Not open yet: 준비 중 (junbi jung).

big.note: 'It's big'. Before a noun: 큰 (keun), as in 큰 사이즈 (keun saijeu), a big size.

good_evening.note: Korean has no special evening greeting; the everyday hello works all day.

good_night.note: Before going to sleep. Casual: 잘 자요 (jal jayo). Leaving at night, just say goodbye.

see_you_later.note: Later the same day. For another day: 다음에 봬요 (daeume bwaeyo) or 또 봬요 (tto bwaeyo).

help.note: In real danger people also shout 사람 살려! (saram sallyeo!)

call_police.note: Emergency numbers in Korea: police 112, fire and ambulance 119.

dont_feel_well.note: Where it hurts: 머리가 아파요 (meoriga apayo), my head hurts.

allergic.note: For example: 땅콩 알레르기 (ttangkong allereugi), peanut allergy.

no_problem.note: Also means 'it's OK' and 'no, thanks'. 'No problem, can do': 문제없어요 (munjeeopseoyo).

maybe.note: As a hesitant reply Koreans often say 글쎄요 (geulsseyo), 'hmm, well…'.

dont_know.note: Plainer: 몰라요 (mollayo), which can sound curt.

dont_like_it.note: Softer: 별로예요 (byeolloyeyo), 'not really'. 싫어요 (sireoyo) is blunt.

welcome.note: Heard in every shop as you walk in. Formal welcome to a group: 환영합니다 (hwanyeonghamnida).

my_family.note: Koreans say 우리 (uri), 'our', not 'my', for family. Humbler: 저희 가족 (jeohui gajok).

mother.note: Mum: 엄마 (eomma). Someone else's mother, politely: 어머님 (eomeonim).

father.note: Dad: 아빠 (appa). Someone else's father, politely: 아버님 (abeonim).

brother.note: Older brother, as a man says it. A woman says: 오빠 (oppa). Younger brother: 남동생 (namdongsaeng).

sister.note: Older sister, as a man says it. A woman says: 언니 (eonni). Younger sister: 여동생 (yeodongsaeng).

child.note: Son: 아들 (adeul). Daughter: 딸 (ttal). In speech often shortened to 애 (ae).

friend.note: Same word for a male or female friend. Koreans mostly use it for people their own age.

this_is_my_friend.note: Same for a female friend. 이쪽 (ijjok), 'this side', is the polite way to point to a person.

are_you_married.note: Answers: 네, 결혼했어요 (ne, gyeolhonhaesseoyo), or 아직이요 (ajigiyo), 'not yet'.

monday.note: 월 (wol) means moon. Every day ends in 요일 (yoil), 'day of the week'.

what_day.note: For the date instead: 오늘 며칠이에요? (oneul myeochirieyo?)

next_week.note: This week: 이번 주 (ibeon ju). Last week: 지난주 (jinanju).

eleven.note: For prices and dates: 십일 (sibil). Before a noun: 열한 (yeolhan).

twelve.note: For prices and dates: 십이 (sibi). Before a noun: 열두 (yeoldu).

twenty.note: For prices and dates: 이십 (isip). Before a noun: 스무 (seumu), as in 스무 살 (seumu sal), age 20.

fifty.note: For prices and dates: 오십 (osip). Native numbers this big are mostly used for ages.

hundred.note: There is no native word in use. Just 백, with no 일 (il), 'one', in front.

thousand.note: Just 천, with no 일 (il) in front. 10,000 has its own word, 만 (man), key for prices.

how_old.note: To someone your age or younger: 몇 살이에요? (myeot sarieyo?). To an elder: 연세가 어떻게 되세요? (yeonsega eotteoke doeseyo?)

years_old.note: Ages use native numbers: 스무 살 (seumu sal), 20; 서른 살 (seoreun sal), 30.

red.note: Before a noun: 빨간 (ppalgan), as in 빨간 차 (ppalgan cha), a red car.

blue.note: Before a noun: 파란 (paran), as in 파란 하늘 (paran haneul), blue sky.

green.note: Also 녹색 (noksaek). A green traffic light is called 파란불 (paranbul), a 'blue light'.

what_colour.note: In a shop: 다른 색 있어요? (dareun saek isseoyo?), do you have other colours?

this_one.note: The 요 (yo) makes it polite. To ask for it: 이거 주세요 (igeo juseyo).

that_one.note: 저거 is far from both of you. Near the person you're talking to: 그거요 (geugeoyo).

another_one.note: Side dishes are refilled free: 이거 더 주세요 (igeo deo juseyo), more of this, please.

its_hot.note: Weather or feeling hot. For hot food or water: 뜨거워요 (tteugeowoyo).

its_cold.note: Weather or feeling cold. For cold food or drinks: 차가워요 (chagawoyo).

weather_today.note: A likely answer: 흐려요 (heuryeoyo), it's cloudy.

beautiful_day.note: Koreans praise the weather, not the day. 좋네요 sounds like 'jon-ne-yo'.

umbrella.note: Asking in a shop: 우산 있어요? (usan isseoyo?)

summer.note: The rainy season, late June to July, is 장마 (jangma).

room.note: Hotels also say 객실 (gaeksil). Room numbers take 호 (ho): 305호, room 305.

luggage.note: Can I leave my bags?: 짐 좀 맡겨도 돼요? (jim jom matgyeodo dwaeyo?)

wifi_password.note: Casual short form: 와이파이 비번 뭐예요? (waipai bibeon mwoyeyo?)

map.note: Show me on the map, please: 지도에서 보여 주세요 (jidoeseo boyeo juseyo).

next_train.note: On the subway: 다음 지하철 언제 와요? (daeum jihacheol eonje wayo?)

is_this_seat_free.note: Literally 'is this seat taken?', so 네 (ne) means taken. Also: 여기 앉아도 돼요? (yeogi anjado dwaeyo?)

what_do_you_do.note: More formal: 직업이 어떻게 되세요? (jigeobi eotteoke doeseyo?)

i_work_in.note: At a bank: 은행에서 일해요 (eunhaengeseo ilhaeyo). In sales: 영업 쪽에서 일해요 (yeongeop jjogeseo ilhaeyo).

im_student.note: Same for men and women. University student: 대학생 (daehaksaeng).

office.note: For your workplace Koreans usually say 회사 (hoesa), 'the company'.

meeting.note: Often pronounced 'hwe-i'. I'm in a meeting: 회의 중이에요 (hoeui jungieyo).

day_off.note: Holiday leave from work: 휴가 (hyuga). A shop's closing day: 휴무 (humu).

colleague.note: Same for men and women. Often 회사 동료 (hoesa dongnyo), 'work colleague'.

lets_start.note: Sounds like the person leading. Softer, to seniors: 시작할까요? (sijakalkkayo?), shall we start?

good_job.note: Also 최고예요! (choegoyeyo!), 'the best!'. At the end of work: 수고하셨습니다 (sugohasyeotseumnida).

table_for_two.note: Your answer to 몇 분이세요? (myeot buniseyo?), how many? Uses native 두 (du), not 이 (i).

what_recommend.note: Literally 'what's tasty here?' – what Koreans really ask. Also: 추천 메뉴가 뭐예요? (chucheon menyuga mwoyeyo?)

not_spicy.note: Less spicy: 덜 맵게 해 주세요 (deol maepge hae juseyo). Is it spicy?: 매워요? (maewoyo?)

vegetarian_food.note: Asking: 채식 메뉴 있어요? (chaesik menyu isseoyo?). I'm vegetarian: 저는 채식주의자예요 (jeoneun chaesikjuuijayeyo).

more_water.note: A sign saying 물은 셀프 (mureun selpeu) means you fetch it yourself.

no_sugar.note: In cafés the sweetener is usually syrup: 시럽 빼 주세요 (sireop ppae juseyo).

im_full.note: To a host offering more: 많이 먹었어요 (mani meogeosseoyo), 'I've eaten a lot'.

takeaway.note: Staff may ask 드시고 가세요? (deusigo gaseyo?), eating here? Answer: 포장이요 (pojangiyo).

it_was_delicious.note: On the way out, the classic thanks is 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeotseumnida).

keep_change.note: Literally 'the change is fine'. Tipping isn't customary in Korea; mostly heard in taxis.

stomach.note: Same word as 'pear' and 'boat'; context makes it clear.

head_hurts.note: Swap in any body part: 배가 아파요 (baega apayo), my stomach hurts.

call_ambulance.note: The ambulance number in Korea is 119.

dentist.note: The dental clinic, as in 'going to the dentist'. The dentist in person: 치과 의사 (chigwa uisa).

need_rest.note: Also: 좀 쉬어야겠어요 (jom swieoyagesseoyo), 'I think I'd better rest'.

get_well.note: Formal, in cards and messages: 쾌유를 빕니다 (kwaeyureul bimnida).

lets_meet.note: Also common: 언제 밥 한번 먹어요 (eonje bap hanbeon meogeoyo), 'let's eat sometime' – often a pleasantry, not a plan.

are_you_free.note: Casual, to friends: 내일 시간 있어? (naeil sigan isseo?)

call_me.note: Text me: 문자 주세요 (munja juseyo). On KakaoTalk: 카톡 주세요 (katok juseyo).

your_number.note: Simpler: 번호 뭐예요? (beonho mwoyeyo?). Digits are read 일, 이, 삼 (il, i, sam), and 0 as 공 (gong).

have_nice_day.note: Casual: 좋은 하루 보내 (joeun haru bonae).

good_luck.note: Before an exam or a big day, Koreans cheer 화이팅! (hwaiting!)

happy_birthday.note: To an elder: 생신 축하드려요 (saengsin chukadeuryeoyo). Casual: 생일 축하해 (saengil chukahae).

miss_you.note: Polite, e.g. to an older relative: 보고 싶어요 (bogo sipeoyo).
